meta.scope: Only ICMR and MoHFW guidelines (MoHFW includes its directorates and programmes: NCVBDC, NCDC, NVHCP, DHR). No WHO, IAP or other-body documents.
meta.how_to_read: Each condition lists first-line tests with the day-of-illness window in which they are valid. Pair differentiators apply when the top two or three conditions are close. Every line carries source ids (see sources) and a section/page locator.

cbc.name: Complete blood count with differential, haematocrit and platelet count

eschar_exam.name: Skin examination for eschar (neck, axillae, chest, abdomen, groin) and lymph nodes

g6pd.name: G6PD status (guides primaquine for P. vivax)

malaria_smear.name: Blood smear for malaria parasite (thick and thin)

blood_culture_2.name: Blood cultures, two sets, before any antibiotic

lepto_rapid.name: Leptospirosis rapid screening test (immunochromatography or slide agglutination)

throat_swab_antigen.name: Throat swab rapid streptococcal antigen test

throat_swab_culture.name: Throat swab culture for group A streptococcus

tb_naat.name: TB nucleic acid amplification test (CBNAAT / Truenat)

dark_field.name: Dark-field microscopy for Leptospira (as a sole test)

common_workup.text: Fever day 1-2: defer investigations and antimicrobials unless the patient has features of sepsis.
Fever day 3-4: blood count with differential, liver and renal function, urine examination, blood sugar, malaria smear and RDT, and a dengue antigen test if suspicion is high.
Fever beyond 5 days: the day 3-4 tests plus two sets of blood cultures and a chest X-ray; add IgM serology for dengue, chikungunya, scrub typhus and leptospirosis according to clinical suspicion.
Fever beyond 7 days: all of the above plus an abdominal ultrasound.

first_line.why: Send for every suspected case; repeat once if the first smear is negative in an endemic area.
Bivalent RDT is used when a microscopy result will not be back within 24 hours; if malaria is still strongly suspected after a negative RDT, also send a slide.

also.why: Primaquine for P. vivax is guided by G6PD status; it is contraindicated in G6PD deficiency, infants and pregnancy.

if_severe.why: Severe malaria needs a smear with parasite count reported within an hour, plus haemoglobin, blood glucose and urine examination; refer to a facility that can give parenteral treatment.
Hypoglycaemia is a complication of severe malaria.
Required in the severe malaria work-up.

first_line.why: NS1 is sent for samples collected on day 1 to 5 of fever; the lab should be told the day of onset and the day of collection.
IgM is sent after day 5; it is usually detectable by day 5 but can appear later.
RT-PCR on acute-phase serum has replaced virus isolation as the standard for detecting virus.
Recommended for all patients with warning signs and all patients with fever beyond 3 days; look for leucopenia, falling platelets and a rising haematocrit.

also.why: Recommended together with the blood count in the same patients.
Adults, patients with comorbidities, shock or complications.
Adults, patients with comorbidities, shock or complications.

if_severe.why: Haematocrit every 4-6 hours in stable cases, more often if unstable; a rise of 10% above baseline is an early sign of plasma leakage.
Chest X-ray or ultrasound helps detect plasma leakage.
Ultrasound helps detect plasma leakage and gall bladder wall thickening.

not_recommended.why: The national programme does not recommend rapid tests for diagnosing dengue or guiding management, because accuracy varies from batch to batch.

notes.text: IgG ELISA indicates past infection only and is not a diagnostic test for acute dengue.

first_line.why: RT-PCR is used between day 0 and day 7 of symptoms (viral RNA is detectable up to about 8 days).
IgM serology is used after day 7; repeat testing in 5 to 10 days if suspicion persists and the first result is negative.
Leucopenia with lymphocyte predominance is usual and severe thrombocytopenia is rare; useful to separate it from dengue.

also.why: ESR is usually raised and CRP rises in the acute phase.
Dengue, malaria and other tropical fevers must be excluded at first contact.

notes.text: Dengue and chikungunya can occur together, so a positive result for one does not exclude the other.

first_line.why: Blood culture is the gold standard; two sets are drawn before empiric antibiotics.
Part of the day 3-4 baseline work-up for undifferentiated fever.

not_recommended.why: Avoid the Widal test for diagnosis; it may also be negative before the second week of fever.

notes.text: Suspect typhoid with continuous fever, gastrointestinal symptoms and splenomegaly.

first_line.why: An eschar is the single most useful clue; look in moist skin folds, where it may lack the black scab. Also look for regional lymphadenopathy and rash.
IgM capture ELISA is the mainstay of laboratory diagnosis; a significant IgM titre appears at the end of the first week (OD cut-off 0.5).
Can be used at primary level only after 5 to 7 days of fever; a titre of 1:80 or more suggests possible infection. Low sensitivity.

also.why: Best on eschar or blood in the first week; available only at a few centres.
Thrombocytopenia is seen in most patients.
Raised transaminases are common, with ALT usually higher than AST.
Bilateral infiltrates are common; pneumonia is a frequent complication.

not_recommended.why: Rapid tests are not recommended for scrub typhus at the present stage.

notes.text: Suspect a rickettsial infection in an undifferentiated fever of 5 days or more; if an eschar is present, a shorter fever can be scrub typhus.

first_line.why: A rapid test is used for screening at PHC and CHC level; results need confirmation by ELISA.
ELISA can detect antibody earlier than MAT and tells recent from past infection; antibody tests are generally positive only after 5-7 days.
Marked CPK elevation points to leptospirosis and helps separate it from viral and alcoholic hepatitis.
Some renal involvement is almost always present: proteinuria, casts, haematuria.

also.why: Gold standard for serovar-specific antibodies; a rising titre between acute and convalescent sera is confirmatory. State or reference laboratory.
Useful in the first days when antibodies are not yet detectable; state or reference laboratory.
Blood culture within 10 days of onset and before antibiotics; slow and specialised.
Transaminases are normal or only mildly raised (hundreds of IU/L).
Urea and creatinine are raised when the kidney is involved.
Neutrophilia and thrombocytopenia are typical.

not_recommended.why: Dark-field microscopy has low sensitivity and specificity and is not recommended as the only test.

notes.text: Leptospira serology cross-reacts with hepatitis A and E, so read serology together with the enzyme pattern and confirm with MAT or PCR where possible.

conditional.if_: Category C features: breathlessness, chest pain, drowsiness, low blood pressure, bluish discolouration, or worsening of a chronic illness
conditional.why: These patients should be tested for influenza (swab RT-PCR) and hospitalised; empirical oseltamivir is started while the result is pending.

notes.text: No influenza test is required for Category A (mild fever with cough or sore throat) or Category B (high-grade fever, severe sore throat, or a high-risk group).

first_line.why: In acute hepatitis with jaundice, bilirubin is above 2.5 mg/dL and ALT is more than 10 times the upper limit of normal.
IgM anti-HAV marks acute hepatitis A; it appears 5-10 days before symptoms and persists up to 6 months.
Definitive diagnosis of hepatitis E rests on IgM anti-HEV; suspect it when hepatitis A is excluded or when several cases cluster.

if_severe.why: Suspect acute liver failure with confusion, persistent vomiting, bleeding or hypoglycaemia; refer when sensorium is altered and INR is above 1.5.
Repeated hypoglycaemia is a warning sign of liver failure.

notes.text: Hepatitis A and E cannot be told apart, or from other viral hepatitis, on clinical grounds alone.

when.text: fever beyond 5 days, or earlier if septic

first_line.why: At least two sets before empiric antibiotics.
White cells, protein and blood point to a urinary source.
Collect before antibiotics when pyelonephritis or urosepsis is possible.
Chest X-ray looks for an occult pneumonia.
Ultrasound looks for hepatic, renal or other intra-abdominal sources.

also.why: Leucocytosis can point to a bacterial source.
Part of the baseline work-up.

if_severe.why: In suspected sepsis, measure lactate and draw blood cultures before antibiotics.

notes.text: The primary source is often occult, most often pneumonia, an intra-abdominal infection or urosepsis, and may be silent in the elderly.

first_line.why: Evidence of a preceding streptococcal infection is essential for the diagnosis: throat antigen or culture positive, or a raised ASO titre.
Same essential criterion as above.
Raised ASO titre (above 320 U) counts as evidence of preceding streptococcal infection.
Minor criteria: ESR above 60 mm/h or CRP 3 mg/dL or more with polyarthralgia; ESR above 30 with monoarthralgia.
A prolonged PR interval for age is a minor criterion unless carditis is already a major criterion.
Monitor for carditis in all patients.

also.why: Total and differential leucocyte count.
Chest X-ray as part of the cardiac assessment.
Optional additional marker of recent streptococcal infection.

notes.text: Think of rheumatic fever when there is migratory arthritis after a significant sore throat.

first_line.why: Chest X-ray in anyone screened positive: cough, fever or significant weight loss/night sweats; also if chest findings are present.
Upfront nucleic acid amplification test (CBNAAT/Truenat) on a sputum sample in those screened positive.

notes.text: Screen for TB with the four-symptom complex: cough or fever for more than 2 weeks, significant weight loss, night sweats. Consider TB in any prolonged undifferentiated fever, especially with weight loss.

pair_differentiators.contrast: Leucopenia, thrombocytopenia and a raised haematocrit are common in dengue and infrequent in chikungunya; bleeding, organ involvement and shock are common in severe dengue and rare in chikungunya; polyarthralgia is frequent in chikungunya and less common in dengue. Both can occur together.

In leptospirosis AST and ALT are normal or only mildly raised and CPK is high; in viral hepatitis ALT is markedly raised and CPK is normal. Leptospira serology cross-reacts with hepatitis A and E, so do not rely on serology alone.

Dengue usually causes a mild to moderate transaminase rise with uncommon jaundice, plus falling platelets and rising haematocrit; acute viral hepatitis shows jaundice with bilirubin above 2.5 mg/dL and ALT above 10 times normal.

Rheumatic fever gives fleeting, migratory arthritis of the large joints, more often in children, after a recent sore throat, with a raised ASO titre and diagnosis by Jones criteria (ECG PR interval, echocardiogram for carditis). Chikungunya gives symmetrical, mainly small-joint polyarthralgia and is confirmed by RT-PCR or IgM.
An eschar, regional lymphadenopathy or rash favours scrub typhus. Both can cause low platelets and mild hepatitis, so serology decides; a rising haematocrit favours dengue.
Eschar and lymphadenopathy point to scrub typhus; conjunctival suffusion, calf muscle tenderness, a high CPK and urine abnormalities point to leptospirosis.

Blood culture serves both. A chest, urinary or abdominal focus on X-ray, urine tests or ultrasound supports secondary bacteraemia; continuous fever with gastrointestinal symptoms and splenomegaly supports typhoid.

Prolonged fever with weight loss or night sweats calls for chest X-ray and NAAT; bacteraemia needs cultures and a search for a focus. Avoid empiric fluoroquinolones where TB is possible, because they can mask TB.
Mild influenza-like illness needs no influenza test (influenza RT-PCR only for Category C), so the useful tests are those for dengue and malaria, which have specific management.
Malaria should be excluded in every acute undifferentiated fever, because it has specific treatment and can coexist with dengue.

default_pair_rule: For a close pair with no explicit entry, send the diagnostic tests of each condition that the other does not share, routine laboratory tests before reference-laboratory tests, filtered to the day of fever when it is known. If nothing remains, send the first-line tests of both.
conflicts: Dengue rapid tests: ICMR 2019 (S04 §2.1.5) lists a dengue rapid NS1 antigen test; NCVBDC 2023 (S02 §6.1.7) does not recommend rapid tests. This protocol follows NCVBDC, the national programme and the later document.

Day 3-4 baseline: ICMR 2019 lists blood count, malaria smear and RDT; the joint NCDC-ICMR 2025 guideline adds liver and renal function, urine examination and blood sugar. This protocol follows the 2025 version.
Dengue NS1 window: NCVBDC 2023 says NS1 for day 1-5 and IgM after day 5; ICMR 2019 says NS1 can diagnose during the first week. This protocol uses NCVBDC.
open_items: TB: the four-symptom screen, chest X-ray and upfront NAAT come from a MoHFW note (S12) read in excerpt. Confirm against the current NTEP Technical and Operational Guidelines, including whether sputum smear remains first-line in your setting and that antibody (serology) tests are not to be used (relayed by secondary summaries only, so not included).
Influenza, rheumatic fever, TB and co-infection sources (S09-S13) were read as excerpts; confirm the exact wording against the full documents.
